evidence.claim: Toketee Falls drops approximately 120 feet in two stages through ancient columnar basalt. Its name comes from Chinook Jargon, meaning pretty or graceful; a 1916 federal naming decision chose Toketee over Ireland Falls and Toketie Falls.
evidence.quote: Carved from ancient columnar basalt, Toketee Falls drops approximately 120 feet (37 m) in two stages.

evidence.claim: Toketee Falls drops approximately 120 feet in two stages through ancient columnar basalt. Its name comes from Chinook Jargon, meaning pretty or graceful; a 1916 federal naming decision chose Toketee over Ireland Falls and Toketie Falls.
evidence.quote: Toketee (pronounced TOKE-uh-tee), is a Chinook Jargon word meaning "pretty" or "graceful". The falls was officially named by a United States Board on Geographic Names decision in 1916, over alternate names Ireland Falls and Toketie Falls.

evidence.claim: The North Umpqua’s flow here is regulated. An upstream dam forms Toketee Lake, and a penstock diverts water to generate electricity, reducing the volume that passes over the falls. The waterfall belongs to both a volcanic landscape and a working hydroelectric system.
evidence.quote: The waterfall is regulated by a dam built just upstream by PacifiCorp, which now regulates and reduces the water flow over the falls as part of the North Umpqua Hydroelectric Project.

evidence.claim: The North Umpqua’s flow here is regulated. An upstream dam forms Toketee Lake, and a penstock diverts water to generate electricity, reducing the volume that passes over the falls. The waterfall belongs to both a volcanic landscape and a working hydroelectric system.
evidence.quote: The damming forms a reservoir called Toketee Lake.

evidence.claim: The North Umpqua’s flow here is regulated. An upstream dam forms Toketee Lake, and a penstock diverts water to generate electricity, reducing the volume that passes over the falls. The waterfall belongs to both a volcanic landscape and a working hydroelectric system.
evidence.quote: Previously the full volume of the North Umpqua River was allowed to flow over the falls, but the flow has been reduced by a penstock that utilizes the drop of the falls to generate hydroelectricity.

evidence.claim: PacifiCorp constructed the North Umpqua Hydroelectric Project between 1947 and 1956, using dams, reservoirs, canals, flumes, penstocks and tunnels.
evidence.quote: The project was constructed by PacifiCorp between 1947 and 1956.

evidence.claim: Mount Thielsen rises east of Diamond Lake, opposite Mount Bailey on the western side.
evidence.quote: It is located between Mount Bailey to the west and Mount Thielsen to the east

evidence.claim: Its pointed summit is the result of erosion: glaciers cut into the old volcano until no summit crater remained and the upper mountain became a horn.
evidence.quote: Thielsen has been so deeply eroded by glaciers that there is no summit crater and the upper part of the mountain is more or less a horn.

evidence.claim: Lightning has added a smaller mark. Strikes melt summit rock into glassy material called fulgurite, found only within the top five to ten feet.
evidence.quote: Fulgurites (substances that form when lightning melts rock) on the volcano are restricted to the very pinnacle of the mountain, and are only found between the top 5 feet (2 m) and 10 feet (3 m) of its summit.

evidence.claim: A United States Geological Survey team studied those deposits in 1884. Mountain hemlock and fir grow up to the timberline. From the lake, the larger feature to notice is the spire itself.
evidence.quote: In 1884 a United States Geological Survey team headed by J. S. Diller began studying the mountains of the Cascade Range. Their intended destinations included Thielsen, which was climbed and sampled for its fulgurite variant.

evidence.claim: A United States Geological Survey team studied those deposits in 1884. Mountain hemlock and fir grow up to the timberline. From the lake, the larger feature to notice is the spire itself.

flags: ODOT recommends five to seven hours; archived FHWA allows eight. Use the road agency’s recommendation with attribution.
Glide cache calls the head-on confluence unique worldwide; ODOT says one of few. Omit both superlatives. Glide moment is short because supported local material is limited.
Toketee height retains the source’s approximately. Hydro regulation prevents presenting the entire corridor as unmodified water.
Mount Thielsen’s existing coordinate and roadside kind are retained, but the coordinate marks the summit, not a turnout. Copy concerns the view from the Diamond Lake area, not summit access.

Thielsen cache alternates Klamath and Chinook historical associations and gives different eruption-age ranges. Those claims are omitted; no Indigenous community source or primary geological paper is cached.
No route-construction campaign is documented; history distinguishes the older wagon road and bridge from the later designated corridor.
The archived FHWA page lacks full page text. Seasonal note is based on cached ODOT guidance, not a live road-condition check.
The current draft’s 30-mile fly-fishing-only restriction is omitted: cached tourism copy supports it, but no current fisheries regulation is supplied.
